heading: Cold open
narration: The world's most famous ugly fish was photographed after it had been ruined.

heading: Cold open
narration: In its own habitat, a blobfish looks like a fairly ordinary deep-sea fish: a large head, a tapering body and visible fins, its soft flesh held in shape by the water around it.

heading: Cold open
narration: NOAA notes that pressure rises by roughly one atmosphere for every ten metres of depth.

heading: Cold open
narration: Near 1000 metres, a depth within the range reported for blobfish, NOAA's rule gives about 100 atmospheres pressing in from every side.

heading: Cold open
narration: You might assume that crushing weight explains the melted face in the famous picture.

heading: Cold open
narration: Mostly, it does not. The face sagged because something far more ordinary was taken away.

heading: The famous face belongs to a dead specimen
narration: The name blobfish is usually applied to Psychrolutes marcidus, one of a group often called fathead sculpins.

heading: The famous face belongs to a dead specimen
narration: It lives over the continental slopes off southeastern Australia and New Zealand, in cold, dark water near the seafloor.

heading: The famous face belongs to a dead specimen
narration: Very few people have ever seen one alive. Most of the images in circulation show specimens on decks, in trays and in jars.

heading: The famous face belongs to a dead specimen
narration: That is not unusual for deep-sea fish. It does mean that the public picture of this species was built from the condition it ends up in, not the condition it lives in. The rest of this story is about closing that gap.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: The common explanation goes like this. The blobfish lives under enormous pressure, so when it comes up, it decompresses and falls apart.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: There is something to that, but it skips a step. Many fish that suffer badly when brought up quickly have a swim bladder, a gas-filled organ used to control buoyancy.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Gas expands as pressure drops, and that expansion can rupture tissue and push organs out of place.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Fathead sculpins like the blobfish are generally described as having no swim bladder.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Their bodies are built largely of gelatinous flesh, watery tissue close to the density of the seawater around it.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Water and watery tissue barely compress, so the pressure change alone does relatively little to them.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: The decisive change comes at the end of the journey. The fish is lifted into air, and gravity flattens the body. That is why the face sags.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Think about what holds a body's shape. In you, muscle and bone do that work against gravity all day.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: In a blobfish, the water does much of it. A body close to neutral buoyancy is supported evenly from every side, so loose skin and gelatinous flesh hold their form without much internal structure.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: Take away that support from surrounding water and nothing replaces it. The tissue slumps, the way a jellyfish does on a beach.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: That is why the body in the famous image spreads out, and why the skin over the snout hangs forward into that nose-like flap.

heading: Pressure is real, but it did not melt the face
narration: The shape was never held by support from muscle and bone. It was borrowed from the ocean.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: It helps to walk through the journey from seabed to photograph in order, because each stage leaves a mark.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: First, the fish is caught in a trawl net and pressed against other animals, rocks and mesh as the net is towed.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: A soft-skinned fish is easily scraped and torn. Second, it is hauled up through the water, passing from cold depths into warmer surface water while pressure falls steadily.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: For a body without gas, this is less dramatic than it is for a fish with a swim bladder, but it is not harmless.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: Third, it is lifted into air, where its buoyant support disappears all at once.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: Finally, it is laid on a flat surface and photographed. Each step distorts the body, and the camera only sees the last one.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: None of this requires guessing about hidden damage. It follows from things that are well established: how gas behaves under pressure, how buoyancy supports a body in water, and what trawling does to soft-skinned animals.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: The specific injuries to the famous specimen are a separate question. Nobody documented them in enough detail to list them one by one.

heading: Every step from seabed to deck changes the body
narration: What can be said is that the photograph is consistent with a fragile body that has lost its support and taken some damage along the way.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: There is a reason the blobfish is built this way, and it has nothing to do with appearance.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: This is what the body design explains. Deep water offers little food, so a body that costs little to build and run has an advantage.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: Gelatinous flesh is mostly water, which is cheap. With no swim bladder, the fish has no gas organ to adjust as its depth changes.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: A body near neutral buoyancy can stay just above the seafloor without spending energy on swimming.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: Little muscle means low running costs. The trade-off is that the fish is not built for speed.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: It is thought to feed largely on small invertebrates that come within reach.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: How it hunts in detail, though, is not well recorded. That part of the checklist stays open.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: Notice what that does to the famous image. Every feature that makes the specimen look grotesque also makes the living fish efficient.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: The loose skin, the soft flesh and the lack of rigid structure add up to a quiet, economical animal in water.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: Out of water they add up to a puddle. The photograph did not reveal an ugly fish.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: It revealed what happens to a body designed for one environment when it is dropped into another.

heading: A cheap body is a good body at depth
narration: That is a real and interesting fact. It is just not the fact most people took from the picture.

heading: What to notice in the edit

heading: What to notice in the edit

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: A fish against dark water, lit from a vehicle above, is being seen in the condition it lives in.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Neither image is false. A photograph is a record of a condition, not a portrait of a species.

heading: What to notice in the edit

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Those are the clearest living images available, so the comparison is made openly, and you should weigh it that way.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: This evidence settles the main point. The famous image shows a damaged specimen out of water, and a living blobfish keeps a recognisable fish shape.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It does not settle every detail of how a living Psychrolutes marcidus looks, from the exact set of its fins to its colour in natural conditions, because direct footage of this species alive is scarce.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Colour in deep-sea footage also depends on the lights the vehicle carries, since almost no sunlight reaches these depths.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Nor does any of this tell you how blobfish behave, how long they live, or whether their numbers are changing.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Those questions need observations that, for this fish, mostly have not been made yet.

heading: Closing
narration: The blobfish became famous for a face it never wore while alive.

heading: Closing
narration: What it actually looks like is quieter: a soft, broad-headed fish resting in cold water, held together by the same ocean that holds it up.

heading: Closing
narration: The ugly picture was real. It simply shows what happens after the water is gone.
